chicken-breast-fried-coated-skin-coating.title: Chicken breast, fried, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast that has been deep‑fried in a crispy coating, served without the edible skin or coating. It is a common item on fast‑food and quick‑service restaurant menus, often presented as strips or nuggets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Deep‑frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden, crunchy crust.
The coating is usually a mixture of flour, breadcrumbs and spices, but it is often discarded by diners who prefer the meat only.
Raw chicken breast is one of the leanest cuts of poultry, yet frying adds a substantial amount of calories.
In the United States this product is frequently called "Chicken Tenders" or "Chicken Strips".
In some countries the coating is served on the side, allowing customers to choose whether to eat it.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low fat in the raw meat
items.content: Raw breast contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, though much of it is absorbed during frying.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B3 (niacin) and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune health and thyroid function.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The high protein content helps keep you feeling full for longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories and fat, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Using old or repeatedly heated oil can introduce trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: The coating often contains salt and flavor enhancers, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten
items.content: The breading typically includes wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried chicken breast strips are usually served hot with dipping sauces such as barbecue, ranch, or honey‑mustard. They can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, or wraps, and the coating can be removed if a lower‑calorie option is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C and consume within 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

chicken-wings-boneless-with-hot-sauce-fr.title: Boneless Chicken Wings with Hot Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Boneless chicken wings coated in a hot sauce are a popular snack item often served in bars and fast‑food restaurants. The chicken meat is tender, while the sauce adds a bold, spicy kick.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Boneless wings are easier to eat because they don’t require bone removal.
Hot sauce is usually made from chili peppers, vinegar, sugar and spices.
In the US they are commonly called "boneless wings" and come with a variety of sauces.
Chicken wings are a staple food during sports broadcasts.
There are many sauce variations: from classic Buffalo to Asian Sriracha.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat when prepared properly
items.content: If baked or grilled without excess oil, boneless wings remain relatively low in fat.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken contains niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The product provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Capsaicin may boost metabolism
items.content: Chili peppers contain capsaicin, which can slightly increase thermogenesis.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Hot sauces often contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Spicy sauce can irritate the stomach
items.content: People with gastritis or ulcer disease should limit consumption.

items.title: Calorie density when fried
items.content: If the wings are deep‑fried, their calorie and fat content rise significantly.

items.title: Sugar in some sauces
items.content: Certain sauce recipes add sugar, increasing the product’s glycemic index.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wings can be served hot as a standalone snack, with celery or carrot sticks, or as part of combo meals. They are hand‑friendly and are often enjoyed with extra dipping sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked wings in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen wings keep for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Coconut oil is extracted from the flesh of mature coconuts (Cocos nucifera). It has a distinctive aroma and a mild sweet taste. The oil is widely used in cooking, cosmetics, and traditional medicine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut oil is high in saturated fatty acids, especially lauric acid.
In tropical countries it is the primary cooking fat.
Lauric acid possesses antimicrobial properties.
Coconut oil can be cold‑pressed (unrefined) or refined.
In some cultures coconut oil is considered an “energy fat” and used in rituals.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Lauric acid may boost the body’s defenses by disrupting bacteria and viruses.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Medium‑chain triglycerides (MCTs) are quickly metabolized into energy, useful for active lifestyles.

items.title: Skin health
items.content: Topical application moisturizes skin, aids minor wound healing, and reduces irritation.

items.title: Hair care
items.content: The oil nourishes hair follicles, reduces breakage, and adds shine.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Tocopherols in the oil help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to coconut oil.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Coconut oil is very calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Not suitable for very high‑heat cooking
items.content: Overheating can cause the oil to form harmful compounds.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use coconut oil for sautéing, baking, adding to smoothies, sauces, and salad dressings. Unrefined oil is great in cold dishes and as a skin or hair mask.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the oil in a tightly sealed container in a cool, dark place. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator to maintain freshness. Discard if it develops a rancid smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried green beans are cooked green bean pods quickly sautéed in vegetable oil until lightly crisp and golden. They retain a crunchy texture and fresh, slightly sweet flavor, often enhanced with aromatic spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are rich in antioxidants such as vitamin C and carotenoids.
Fried green beans are a staple in many Asian cuisines, especially Chinese and Japanese dishes.
The quick frying process locks in color and crunch by evaporating excess moisture.
Common seasonings include garlic, ginger, soy sauce, chili, and toasted sesame.
Green beans provide a good amount of plant‑based protein and dietary fiber.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 100 g serving of fried green beans contains about 120 kcal, making it diet‑friendly.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Protein contributes to muscle maintenance, especially for vegetarians.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When seasoned with salt or soy sauce, sodium levels can rise; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Gas‑forming compounds
items.content: Beans contain oligosaccharides that may cause bloating in sensitive people.

items.title: Raw bean toxicity
items.content: Uncooked pods contain phytohemagglutinins, so they must be fully cooked before frying.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried green beans can be served as a snack, tossed into salads, added to rice or noodle dishes, or used as a side for meat and fish. Sprinkle with sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, or fresh herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fried green beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them refrigerated, where they stay crisp and flavorful for up to two weeks.

content.title: About
content.content: Sugar cane beverage is a refreshing non‑alcoholic drink made by extracting juice from sugar cane, filtering it, and optionally sweetening or diluting it. The drink has a light sweet taste, a characteristic cane aroma, and can be either carbonated or still.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cane juice has been used in traditional tropical drinks long before colonial times.
Unlike refined sugar, cane juice retains some vitamins and minerals such as vitamin C and potassium.
Cane juice is often the base for fermented drinks, for example, cane kvass.
In some countries the beverage is served chilled with lime or mint to enhance flavor.
Production requires rapid processing to prevent oxidation and darkening of the juice.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Cane juice contains vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The beverage contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s hydration levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in cane juice may provide protection against oxidative stress.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The drink can contain high levels of simple sugars, which is unfavorable for people with diabetes or those trying to lose weight.

items.title: Cane allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cane components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: If the juice is not properly pasteurized, there is a risk of bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The beverage can be enjoyed chilled on its own, used in cocktails, mixed with fruit juices, or added to dessert sauces. For extra zest, lime, mint, or ginger are often added.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the drink in the refrigerator at 0 °C to 4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Keep away from direct sunlight to prevent darkening and flavor loss.

content.title: About
content.content: A wine cooler is a household appliance designed to maintain the optimal storage temperature for wine. It provides a stable climate, protecting wine from sudden temperature swings and preserving its aroma and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Modern wine coolers often feature dual zones, allowing red and white wines to be stored at different temperatures.
Some models are equipped with UV‑protective glass to prevent flavor degradation from light exposure.
Quiet compressors make it possible to place the cooler in a living or dining room without noticeable noise.
Energy consumption of contemporary units is usually below 100 W, making them economical to run.

items.title: Preserves antioxidants
items.content: Proper wine storage retains polyphenols and resveratrol, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Optimal temperatures (12‑14 °C for reds, 8‑10 °C for whites) prevent the growth of unwanted microbes.

items.title: Overheating
items.content: Improper ventilation can cause the compressor to overheat and fail.

items.title: Electrical safety
items.content: Do not place the cooler near water sources without proper grounding and protection.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Place bottles on the shelves without overfilling them to allow air circulation. Select the desired temperature zone and let the unit stabilize before loading.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Position the cooler in a dry area away from direct sunlight. If not used for an extended period, disconnect power and clean the interior shelves of dust.
